title: Sink vs. diagonal patterns as mechanisms for attention switch and oversmoothing prevention
claim: Across layers and models, the first token's embedding is consistently negatively aligned with all other token embeddings, which is the geometric precondition for sinks.
layout: Single wide panel, layer index on x-axis, grouped box plots, red zero reference line
description: A single wide box-and-whisker plot. The x-axis is Transformer layer, from 0 to 31. The y-axis is cosine similarity to the BOS token, from about -0.6 to 0.75. Each layer has up to three small boxes with whiskers, in blue for Gemma, orange for GPT-2 and green for Llama-3.1. A horizontal red line at zero is the reference, and a legend sits at the top center. Nearly all boxes fall below zero, mostly around -0.1 to -0.2. GPT-2 (orange) goes much more negative, to about -0.5, in layers 2 to 9. Layer 0 and a few outliers, such as GPT-2 layer 0 and Gemma layer 27, have long whiskers that reach above zero. The eye goes first to the red zero line and the cluster of boxes just under it.
caption: Cosine similarity between BOS and all other 256 token embeddings at the input to the attention layer, pooled across heads and 50 sequences across 4 language datasets (TinyStories \protect[ref], tinyshakespeare \protect[ref], WikiText \protect[ref], and CodeSearchNet-Python \protect[ref]). The whiskers of the box plot point to absolute minimum and maximum.
abstract: This paper studies the role of sinks and diagonal patterns as attention switch and anti-oversmoothing mechanisms. We analyze geometric conditions under which sinks can be represented, showing a necessary alignment between the embedding of the sink and all other embeddings. Next, we refine the current understanding of the role of sinks in oversmoothing prevention: we specify the conditions under which dense attention is expected to smooth more than sparse attention, and empirically verify that such conditions are often satisfied in practice. We further prove an equivalence between sinks and hard attention switch, in which the output of the attention is identically 0. Finally, we relax the hard attention switch by allowing token self-communication: we provide a quantitative comparison of the costs of representing sinks vs.\ diagonal patterns, showing why sinks are favored in pretrained transformers. The introduction and analysis of diagonal patterns and the generalization of the attention switch close the gap between what oversmoothing prevention requires and what sinks provide, while also establishing when and why attention layers act like MLPs if token communication is not necessary.
